intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that cerebellar ataxia, impaired intellectual development, and dysequilibrium syndrome-4 (CAMRQ4) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the ATP8A2 gene (605870) on chromosome 13q12.

paragraphs.text: Onat et al. (2013) described cerebellar ataxia, mental retardation, and dysequilibrium syndrome as a rare and heterogeneous condition. CAMRQ4 is an autosomal recessive disorder with onset at birth or in infancy. Its main features are cerebellar ataxia, impaired intellectual development, and cerebellar atrophy, and some patients walk on all fours (quadrupedal locomotion). Severity varies: some patients have severe developmental delay, hypotonia, and involuntary movements, while others have congenital ataxia with near normal cognition.

paragraphs.text: Mohamadian et al. (2020) reported 3 affected sibs born to healthy first-cousin parents of Arab descent in an Iranian family. The proband, a 9-year-old girl, first showed severe neonatal hypotonia, followed by delay in all psychomotor and developmental milestones. She was wheelchair-bound and could not walk, sit, or hold her head, and she had had feeding difficulties since infancy. She did not have seizures, optic atrophy, or hearing impairment, and her metabolic investigations were normal. Her affected brother and sister were 17 and 15 years old and had features similar to the proband's. All 3 patients had limited intellectual function with IQ levels from 20 to 40, delayed speech and language, dysarthria, and absent deep tendon reflexes. Brain MRI showed cerebellar atrophy, and hearing examination showed no significant impairment.

paragraphs.text: Narishige et al. (2022) reported 2 Japanese sibs who developed athetotic movements at 1 and 2 months of age. They also had ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, feeding difficulty, hypotonia, and severely delayed development. One of them had retinal degeneration and optic atrophy. Over time, both developed areflexia and flattened auditory brainstem responses. At last follow-up, neither patient could sit or control their head, but some nonverbal communication remained.

paragraphs.text: Ozcelik et al. (2008) studied 4 large consanguineous Turkish kindreds with quadrupedal gait (Unertan syndrome), a rare phenotype associated with dysarthric speech, mental retardation, and varying degrees of cerebrocerebellar hypoplasia. In 2 of the families, the trait mapped to chromosome 9p24 and was caused by mutations in the VLDLR gene. In the other 2 families, the phenotype was not linked to chromosome 9p. The authors concluded that hereditary disorders with quadrupedal gait in humans are genetically heterogeneous. In a reply to Herz et al. (2008) and Humphrey et al. (2008), Ozcelik et al. (2008) discussed the genetic heterogeneity of cerebellar hypoplasia with quadrupedal locomotion.

paragraphs.text: Onat et al. (2013) studied the consanguineous Turkish family with CAMRQ4. They performed targeted next-generation sequencing in an affected individual and followed it with segregation analysis, population screening, and prediction analyses. This identified a homozygous I376M mutation in the ATP8A2 gene, located in the shared homozygous region on chromosome 13q12. The variant lies in a highly conserved C-terminal transmembrane region of the E1-E2 ATPase domain.

paragraphs.text: Mohamadian et al. (2020) studied 3 affected sibs from a consanguineous Iranian family with CAMRQ4 and identified a homozygous c.1339G-A transition in ATP8A2, resulting in a gly447-to-arg (G447R) substitution. The mutation segregated with the disorder: it was homozygous in the 3 affected sibs, heterozygous in both parents and 2 healthy sibs, and absent from 1 healthy sib. It was not found in public databases or in 100 ethnically matched controls, and the authors classified it as likely pathogenic under ACMG criteria. Gly447 lies in a highly conserved part of the cytoplasmic N (ATP-binding) domain. Homology modeling predicted that the substitution greatly reduces protein stability and alters the ligand-binding pocket.

paragraphs.text: Damásio et al. (2021) used exome sequencing in 2 sibs with congenital ataxia and identified a homozygous c.1580-18C-G variant in intron 17 of ATP8A2. In a minigene assay in HEK293T cells, the variant caused use of an alternative acceptor splice site. The resulting aberrant transcript kept 17 bp of intron 17, which inserted 4 amino acids and led to a premature stop codon.

paragraphs.text: Onat et al. (2013) studied 4 affected members of a consanguineous Turkish family with CAMRQ4, who had cerebellar ataxia, mental retardation, dysequilibrium, cerebellar atrophy, and quadrupedal locomotion. In this family they identified a homozygous ile376-to-met (I376M) mutation in the ATP8A2 gene. The mutation was found by targeted next-generation sequencing and supported by segregation analysis, population screening, and prediction analyses. It lies in a highly conserved C-terminal transmembrane region of the E1-E2 ATPase domain.

paragraphs.text: Mohamadian et al. (2020) studied 3 sibs with CAMRQ4 from a consanguineous Iranian family of Arab descent. They identified a homozygous c.1339G-A transition in the ATP8A2 gene, resulting in a gly447-to-arg (G447R) substitution in a highly conserved part of the cytoplasmic N (ATP-binding) domain. The parents and 2 healthy sibs were heterozygous. The variant was absent from public databases and from 100 ethnically matched controls. Homology modeling predicted that it reduces protein stability and alters the ligand-binding pocket.
